GEN.title: The first book of Moses, called Genesis
GEN.writer: Moses, as Jewish and Christian tradition holds. Jesus speaks of the Law as the book of Moses (Mark 12:26). Many scholars think it was put together from older accounts over a longer time.
GEN.when: It tells of the time from creation to Joseph, about 1800 BC. Tradition places the writing in the time of Moses, about 1400 BC.
GEN.to: The people of Israel, to know where they come from and who their God is.
GEN.why: To show that the one God made everything good, that sin came in through people, and that God chose Abraham's family to bring blessing to all nations.
GEN.summary: Genesis means “beginning”. It tells how God created the world and people, how sin and death came in, and how God judged and yet kept His promise. Then it follows one family: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph, whom God leads and keeps.
themes: God is the Creator, and all He made was very good (1:31).
Sin breaks our bond with God and with each other, but God does not let go.
God's covenant with Abraham: a land, a people, and blessing for all nations (12:1-3).
God turns evil into good (50:20).
parts: The beginning: creation, the fall, the flood and Babel
Joseph: from the pit to the palace
GEN.christ: The promise that the woman's offspring will crush the serpent's head (3:15) is the first hint of the Saviour. All nations are blessed through Abraham's offspring, who is Christ (Galatians 3:16).

EXO.title: The second book of Moses, called Exodus
EXO.writer: Moses, as tradition holds. He led the people out of Egypt and wrote down the words of the Lord (24:4).
EXO.when: It tells of Israel's slavery in Egypt, the way out (about 1446 BC; some date it about 1260 BC) and the first year in the desert.
EXO.to: Israel, the people God set free and bound to Himself.
EXO.why: To show the God who hears His people's cry, saves them, gives them His law and comes to live among them.
EXO.summary: Exodus means “going out”. God calls Moses at the burning bush, sends the plagues on Egypt, and leads His people out on the night of the Passover and through the Red Sea. At Mount Sinai He makes a covenant with them and gives the Ten Commandments. The book ends with the tabernacle, the tent where God's glory lives among His people.
themes: God saves: He hears, comes down and sets free (3:7-8).
The Passover: the blood of the lamb protects from death (12:13).
The covenant and the law: God's people live by His word.
God lives among His people in the tabernacle (40:34).
parts: Out of Egypt: Moses, the plagues, the Passover, the Red Sea
At Mount Sinai: the covenant and the Ten Commandments
The golden calf, and God's mercy
The tabernacle built and filled with God's glory
EXO.christ: Christ is our Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7). As Moses led the people out of slavery, Jesus frees us from sin. In Him God lives among us (John 1:14).

LEV.title: The third book of Moses, called Leviticus
LEV.line: A holy God among His people
LEV.writer: Moses, as tradition holds. Most of the book is what the Lord spoke to Moses at Mount Sinai (1:1; 27:34).
LEV.when: Given at Mount Sinai, in the year after Israel left Egypt.
LEV.to: The priests from the tribe of Levi, and all Israel.
LEV.why: To show how a holy God can live among a sinful people: by sacrifice, by cleansing and by a holy life.
LEV.summary: Leviticus is named after the Levites, the tribe of the priests. It sets out the sacrifices, the work of the priests, what is clean and unclean, the great Day of Atonement and the feasts of the year. Its call is: “You shall be holy, for I am holy” (11:44).
themes: God is holy, and calls His people to be holy (11:44).
Sacrifice: sin is serious, and life must be given for it (17:11).
The Day of Atonement: once a year the sins of the people are covered (chapter 16).
Love your neighbour as yourself (19:18).
parts: A holy life and the feasts of the Lord
LEV.christ: Jesus Christ is both the High Priest and the sacrifice. He gave Himself once for all, and His blood brings full forgiveness (Hebrews 9:11-14; 10:10).

NUM.title: The fourth book of Moses, called Numbers
NUM.writer: Moses, as tradition holds. He kept a record of the stages of the journey (33:2).
NUM.when: It covers about 38 years in the desert, from Mount Sinai to the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho.
NUM.to: Israel, and the generation that would enter the promised land.
NUM.why: To show God's faithfulness to an unfaithful people, and that unbelief keeps people out of what God promised.
NUM.summary: Numbers takes its name from the two counts of the people (chapters 1 and 26). Israel sets out from Sinai, but at the border of Canaan the people do not trust God. So that generation wanders in the desert until it has died. God still leads them, feeds them and keeps His promise for their children.
themes: God goes ahead of His people in the cloud and the fire (9:15-23).
Unbelief and grumbling have consequences (chapter 14).
God provides, and stays faithful when people are not.
The priestly blessing: “The Lord bless you and keep you” (6:24-26).
parts: At Sinai: ready for the journey
In the desert: grumbling, unbelief and forty years
On the plains of Moab: Balaam and a new generation
NUM.christ: Jesus said: as Moses lifted up the bronze serpent in the desert, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, that whoever believes in Him may have eternal life (John 3:14-15).

DEU.title: The fifth book of Moses, called Deuteronomy
DEU.writer: Moses spoke these words to Israel before his death (1:1). The last chapter, on his death, was added by another hand; Jewish tradition names Joshua.
DEU.when: Spoken on the plains of Moab at the end of the forty years, just before Israel crossed the Jordan.
DEU.to: The new generation, about to enter the promised land.
DEU.why: To renew the covenant: to remember what God did, and to love and obey Him in the land.
DEU.summary: Deuteronomy means “second law”: Moses repeats and explains the law for the new generation. In three great speeches he reminds them of God's faithfulness, calls them to love God with all their heart, and sets before them life and blessing, or death and curse. The book ends with Moses' song and blessing, and his death on Mount Nebo.
themes: Hear, O Israel: the Lord is one; love Him with all your heart (6:4-5).
Remember: do not forget the Lord when life is good (8:11-18).
Choose life (30:19).
God promises a prophet like Moses (18:15).
parts: Moses' last words, his song and his death
DEU.christ: Jesus answered the tempter three times with words from Deuteronomy (Matthew 4:1-11). He is the prophet like Moses whom God promised (Acts 3:22).

JOS.title: The book of Joshua
JOS.writer: Jewish tradition names Joshua, who wrote some of it himself (24:26). The account of his death was added later.
JOS.when: It tells of Israel's entry into Canaan after Moses' death, about 1400 BC (some date it about 1220 BC).
JOS.to: Israel in the land, to remember how they received it.
JOS.why: To show that God keeps His promises: He gave the land as He swore to the fathers (21:43-45).
JOS.summary: Joshua, Moses' helper, leads the people across the Jordan. The walls of Jericho fall, and the land is taken in battles in which God fights for Israel. Then the land is shared among the tribes. In his last speech Joshua calls the people to choose whom they will serve.
themes: Be strong and of good courage, for God is with you (1:9).
God fights for His people; victory comes by faith and obedience.
Not one of God's promises failed (21:45).
Choose this day whom you will serve (24:15).
parts: Taking the land: Jericho and the battles
The land shared among the tribes
JOS.christ: Joshua and Jesus are the same name: “the Lord saves”. Joshua led the people into the land; Jesus leads God's people into the true rest (Hebrews 4:8-10).

JDG.title: The book of Judges
JDG.writer: The writer is not named; Jewish tradition names Samuel. The words “in those days there was no king in Israel” (17:6) suggest it was written in the time of the kings.
JDG.when: It tells of the time between Joshua and the first king, about 300 years (roughly 1380 to 1050 BC).
JDG.to: Israel, to learn from its history.
JDG.why: To show what happens when people forget God, and how God sends a deliverer again and again when they cry to Him.
JDG.summary: After Joshua dies, Israel turns away from God. The same circle comes back again and again: the people sin, enemies oppress them, they cry to God, and He raises up a judge to save them, such as Deborah, Gideon and Samson. Then they fall away again. The book ends in dark times: “everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (21:25).
themes: Forgetting God leads to trouble (2:10-15).
God hears the cry of His people and saves (2:16).
God uses weak and unlikely people (Gideon, 6:15).
People need a true king who leads them to God.
parts: Israel does not finish the task
The judges: Othniel, Ehud, Deborah, Gideon, Jephthah, Samson and others
Everyone does what is right in his own eyes
JDG.christ: The judges saved for a time, and all of them had faults. They point to Jesus, the Saviour who saves for ever, and the King who rules in righteousness.

RUT.title: The book of Ruth
RUT.writer: The writer is not named; Jewish tradition names Samuel. Since it ends with David's family line, it was written in David's time or later.
RUT.when: The story happens in the time of the judges (1:1).
RUT.to: Israel, to show how God led David's family.
RUT.why: To show God's quiet care in ordinary life, and that He welcomes a stranger who trusts Him.
RUT.summary: Naomi loses her husband and her sons in Moab. Her daughter-in-law Ruth, a Moabite, stays with her: “Your people shall be my people, and your God, my God” (1:16). In Bethlehem Ruth gathers grain in the field of Boaz. Boaz, a relative, redeems the family's land and marries Ruth. Their great-grandson is King David.
themes: Faithful love: Ruth to Naomi, Boaz to Ruth, and God to all of them.
God works quietly in ordinary days.
The redeemer buys back what was lost (chapter 4).
God welcomes people from other nations (2:12).
parts: Naomi and Ruth: loss and loyalty
Ruth in the field of Boaz
Boaz redeems; the line of David
RUT.christ: Boaz the redeemer points to Christ, who paid the price to redeem us. Ruth is named in the family line of Jesus (Matthew 1:5).

1SA.title: The first book of Samuel
1SA.writer: The writer is not named. Samuel, Nathan and Gad kept records (1 Chronicles 29:29), and the book was put together later from them.
1SA.when: It tells of the time from Samuel's birth to Saul's death, about 1100 to 1010 BC.
1SA.why: To show how Israel got a king, and that God looks at the heart.
1SA.summary: Hannah prays for a son and gives Samuel to the Lord. Samuel becomes prophet and judge. The people ask for a king, and God gives them Saul, but Saul does not obey. God chooses David, a shepherd boy, who defeats Goliath. Saul hunts David, yet David will not harm the Lord's anointed. Saul dies in battle.
themes: God hears prayer (Hannah, chapter 1).
To obey is better than sacrifice (15:22).
The Lord looks at the heart (16:7).
The battle is the Lord's (17:47).
1SA.christ: David, the shepherd king from Bethlehem, points to Jesus, the Son of David and the good Shepherd. Hannah's song (chapter 2) sounds again in Mary's song (Luke 1:46-55).

2SA.title: The second book of Samuel
2SA.writer: The writer is not named. It continues 1 Samuel and was put together from the records of prophets such as Nathan and Gad.
2SA.when: It tells of David's forty years as king, about 1010 to 970 BC.
2SA.why: To show David's reign: its blessing, his sin and repentance, and God's promise of a King for ever.
2SA.summary: David becomes king, first over Judah, then over all Israel, and makes Jerusalem his city. God promises that his house and his kingdom will last for ever (chapter 7). Then David sins with Bathsheba and has her husband Uriah killed. The prophet Nathan confronts him, and David repents. Trouble follows in his family, with Absalom's revolt, but God keeps His promise.
themes: God's covenant with David: a King for ever (7:12-16).
Even a man after God's heart can fall into deep sin.
True repentance finds forgiveness (12:13; Psalm 51).
Sin has consequences, even when it is forgiven.
2SA.christ: God's promise to David is fulfilled in Jesus, the Son of David, whose kingdom has no end (Luke 1:32-33).

1KI.title: The first book of the Kings
1KI.writer: The writer is not named; Jewish tradition names Jeremiah. It draws on older records, such as “the book of the acts of Solomon” (11:41), and was completed in the exile in Babylon.
1KI.when: It tells of about 120 years, from Solomon (about 970 BC) to King Ahab and the prophet Elijah (about 850 BC).
1KI.to: God's people in exile, asking why they lost the land.
1KI.why: To show that blessing follows faithfulness to God, and that turning to idols leads to ruin.
1KI.summary: Solomon asks God for wisdom and builds the temple, but in his old age his heart turns to other gods. After him the kingdom splits in two: Israel in the north and Judah in the south. Most of the kings do evil. God sends prophets, above all Elijah, who stands against Ahab, Jezebel and the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel.
themes: The temple: God puts His name among His people (8:27-30).
Wisdom is a gift of God (3:9).
A divided heart divides a kingdom (11:4).
The Lord, He is God (18:39), and He speaks in a still small voice (19:12).
parts: Solomon: wisdom, the temple and his fall
The kingdom divides: Israel and Judah
1KI.christ: Jesus is greater than Solomon (Matthew 12:42) and greater than the temple (Matthew 12:6). Elijah stands with Him on the mountain of the transfiguration (Matthew 17:3).

2KI.title: The second book of the Kings
2KI.line: Elisha, and the road to exile
2KI.writer: The same writer as 1 Kings, of which it is the second half. It was completed in the exile in Babylon, after 560 BC (25:27).
2KI.when: It tells of about 300 years, from Elisha (about 850 BC) to the fall of Jerusalem (586 BC) and after.
2KI.why: To explain why Israel and Judah went into exile: they would not listen to God's prophets. Yet it ends with hope for David's line (25:27-30).
2KI.summary: Elijah is taken up into heaven, and Elisha carries on his work with many miracles, such as the healing of Naaman. The northern kingdom keeps turning to idols and falls to Assyria in 722 BC. Judah has some good kings, such as Hezekiah and Josiah, but at last falls to Babylon. Jerusalem and the temple are destroyed in 586 BC.
themes: God sends prophets again and again before He judges (17:13).
Faithful kings bring renewal: Hezekiah's prayer, Josiah's reform.
Exile is the fruit of a broken covenant.
God keeps a remnant, and a hope.
parts: The fall of the northern kingdom
Judah alone: Hezekiah, Josiah and the fall of Jerusalem
2KI.christ: Jesus names the healing of Naaman as a sign of God's grace to the nations (Luke 4:27). Elisha feeding many with a little bread (4:42-44) points ahead to the miracles of Jesus.

1CH.title: The first book of the Chronicles
1CH.writer: Jewish tradition names Ezra the scribe. The writer used many older records and wrote after the return from exile.
1CH.when: Written about 450 to 400 BC; it looks back from Adam to the end of David's reign.
1CH.to: The people who came back from Babylon to rebuild.
1CH.why: To remind them that they are still God's people, with David's line and the temple at the centre.
1CH.summary: The book begins with long family lists, from Adam to the returned exiles, to show that God's people go on. Then it tells of David: how he brings the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem, receives God's promise, and prepares everything for the temple: the materials, the priests, the Levites and the singers.
themes: God's people have a history and a future.
Worship at the centre: the ark, the music, the temple (chapters 15–16).
God's covenant with David (chapter 17).
We give to God from what He gave us (29:14).
parts: Family lines: from Adam to the return
David becomes king and brings the ark to Jerusalem
1CH.christ: The family lines lead to David, and through David to Jesus Christ (Matthew 1:1). God's promise of a son of David whose throne lasts for ever is fulfilled in Him.

2CH.title: The second book of the Chronicles
2CH.writer: The same writer as 1 Chronicles, of which it is the second half; Jewish tradition names Ezra.
2CH.when: Written about 450 to 400 BC; it tells of Solomon, the kings of Judah, the exile, and the decree of King Cyrus (538 BC).
2CH.why: To show that when God's people seek Him and humble themselves, He hears and restores.
2CH.summary: Solomon builds and dedicates the temple, and God's glory fills it. After the kingdom splits, the book follows only the kings of Judah, of David's line. When kings seek God, such as Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah and Josiah, there is renewal; when they forsake Him, there is decline. It ends with the exile and the decree of Cyrus that the temple may be built again.
themes: If My people humble themselves and pray, I will hear (7:14).
The eyes of the Lord look for those whose heart is loyal to Him (16:9).
The battle is not yours but God's (20:15).
God's mercy: the way back stays open (Manasseh, 33:12-13).
parts: The kings of Judah: seeking God or forsaking Him
Hezekiah, Josiah, the exile and the way back
2CH.christ: The temple, filled with God's glory, points to Christ, in whom God's glory lives among us (John 1:14; 2:19-21).

EZR.title: The book of Ezra
EZR.writer: Ezra, a priest and a scribe skilled in the law of Moses (7:6), as Jewish tradition holds. Parts are written in his own words.
EZR.when: It covers about 80 years after the return from exile, from 538 BC to about 457 BC.
EZR.why: To show how God keeps His word: He moves a heathen king to send His people home, the temple is rebuilt, and the people return to His law.
EZR.summary: King Cyrus of Persia lets the Jews go home. Under Zerubbabel they rebuild the temple, in spite of opposition, and finish it in 516 BC. Many years later Ezra comes to Jerusalem to teach the law. He finds that many have married women who serve other gods, and he leads the people in confession and renewal.
themes: God moves the hearts of kings (1:1).
Rebuilding the house of God (chapters 3–6).
God's word at the centre: Ezra studied it, lived it and taught it (7:10).
Confession and renewal (chapters 9–10).
parts: The return and the rebuilt temple
Ezra brings the law; the people renewed
EZR.christ: The return from exile and the rebuilt temple point to Christ, who brings people home to God and is Himself the true temple (John 2:19-21).

NEH.title: The book of Nehemiah
NEH.writer: Nehemiah, cupbearer to the king of Persia, who tells much of it in his own words (1:1).
NEH.when: About 445 to 430 BC, some years after Ezra came to Jerusalem.
NEH.to: The people in Jerusalem and Judah.
NEH.why: To show how God's people, with prayer and work, rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem and renewed their covenant with God.
NEH.summary: Nehemiah hears that the walls of Jerusalem are broken down. He prays, and the king sends him to rebuild them. In spite of mockery and threats, the walls are finished in 52 days (6:15). Ezra reads the law to the people. They weep, then rejoice, confess their sins and renew the covenant.
themes: Prayer and work go together (2:4; 4:9).
God's word read and explained to the people (8:8).
The joy of the Lord is your strength (8:10).
Renewing the covenant (chapters 9–10).
parts: The law read; the covenant renewed
NEH.christ: Nehemiah left the king's palace to rebuild what was broken down. Christ left His glory to restore what sin had broken.

EST.title: The book of Esther
EST.writer: The writer is not named. It was someone who knew the Persian court well; some name Mordecai.
EST.when: The story happens in Persia under King Ahasuerus (Xerxes), about 483 to 473 BC.
EST.to: Jews in the Persian empire and in Judah. It explains the feast of Purim.
EST.why: To show how God protects His people, even where His name is not spoken.
EST.summary: Esther, a young Jewish woman, becomes queen of Persia. Haman, the king's highest official, plots to kill all the Jews. Mordecai urges Esther to speak: “Who knows whether you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” (4:14). At the risk of her life she goes to the king. Haman's plot falls back on himself, and the Jews are saved. The feast of Purim remembers this.
themes: God's hidden hand: His name does not appear in the book, yet He is at work.
Courage at the right time (4:14-16).
The proud fall and the humble are lifted up.
Sorrow turned into joy (9:22).
parts: The plot turns; the Jews saved; Purim
EST.christ: Esther risked her life and stood between her people and death. Christ did more: He gave His life to save His people.

JOB.title: The book of Job
JOB.writer: The writer is not named. Jewish tradition names Moses; others think of the time of Solomon.
JOB.when: Not known. Job lives like Abraham did: a herdsman whose wealth is his cattle, and who brings sacrifices himself.
JOB.why: To wrestle with the question why the righteous suffer, and to show that God is wise and good even when we do not understand.
JOB.summary: Job is a righteous man who loses his children, his wealth and his health. His three friends say he must have sinned. Job holds on to his innocence and cries out to God. Then God speaks from the storm and shows him the wonders of creation. Job bows before God, and God restores him.
themes: Suffering is not always punishment for sin.
Faith that holds on in the dark: “I know that my Redeemer lives” (19:25).
God's wisdom is far above ours (chapters 38–41).
God is good, and He restores (42:10).
JOB.christ: Job longs for someone to stand between God and himself (9:33) and for a Redeemer who lives (19:25). Jesus is that Mediator (1 Timothy 2:5): the innocent One who suffered for others.

PSA.title: The book of Psalms
PSA.writer: Many writers. 73 psalms are headed “of David”; others are by Asaph, the sons of Korah, Solomon, Moses (Psalm 90) and writers who are not named.
PSA.when: Written over some 500 years, from the time of Moses and David (about 1000 BC) to after the exile, and gathered into five books.
PSA.to: Israel at worship, and every believer who prays.
PSA.why: To give God's people words for every situation: praise, thanks, lament, confession and trust.
PSA.summary: The Psalms are Israel's book of hymns and prayers (CNAC 1.2.2). They praise God as Creator and King, thank Him for His help, cry out in pain and fear, confess sin, and trust Him in all things. The book has five parts, each ending in praise, and closes with “Let everything that has breath praise the Lord” (150:6).
themes: Praise: God is great and good (Psalm 103).
Lament: we may bring our pain to God (Psalm 13).
Trust: the Lord is my shepherd (Psalm 23).
The King: God's anointed reigns (Psalms 2 and 110).
parts: Book 2: the sons of Korah and David
Book 3: Asaph; questions in hard times
Book 5: thanks and praise; the songs of going up
PSA.christ: Jesus prayed the Psalms, even on the cross (22:1; 31:5). He said they speak of Him (Luke 24:44): the King (Psalm 2), the One who suffers (Psalm 22) and the One who rises (16:10).

PRO.title: The Proverbs
PRO.writer: Mostly Solomon (1:1; 10:1), with the sayings of other wise men, of Agur (chapter 30) and of King Lemuel (chapter 31). The men of King Hezekiah copied some of them (25:1).
PRO.when: Solomon's sayings date from about 950 BC; the collection was finished in Hezekiah's time, about 700 BC.
PRO.to: Young people, and all who want to live wisely.
PRO.why: To teach wisdom for everyday life: how to live well before God and with people.
PRO.summary: Proverbs are short, wise sayings. The book begins with a father's lessons for his son, and with Wisdom calling in the streets. Then come hundreds of sayings on work, words, money, family, friendship and pride. Its foundation is: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge” (1:7).
themes: The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom (1:7).
Trust in the Lord, not in your own understanding (3:5-6).
Words have power: death and life are in the tongue (18:21).
Hard work, honesty and humility.
parts: More sayings of Solomon, copied by Hezekiah's men
Agur, Lemuel and the capable wife
PRO.christ: Christ is the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24, 30). In Him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3).

ECC.title: Ecclesiastes, or the Preacher
ECC.writer: “The Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem” (1:1), by tradition Solomon in his old age. Many scholars think it was written later, in Solomon's name.
ECC.when: If Solomon wrote it, about 935 BC; many scholars date it later.
ECC.to: All who ask what life is for.
ECC.why: To show that life without God is empty, and that true meaning lies in fearing God and enjoying His gifts.
ECC.summary: “Vanity of vanities, all is vanity” (1:2): like a breath, everything passes. The Preacher tries wisdom, pleasure, work and wealth, and finds that none of it lasts “under the sun”. Yet he sees life as a gift from God's hand: enjoy it, work, and remember your Creator. His conclusion: “Fear God and keep His commandments” (12:13).
themes: Life under the sun passes like a breath (1:2).
There is a time for everything (3:1-8).
Enjoy God's gifts with thanks (5:18-19).
Fear God, for He will judge (12:13-14).
parts: All is vanity: the search for meaning
ECC.christ: The emptiness the Preacher describes is answered in Christ, who gives life that does not pass away (John 10:10).

SNG.title: The Song of Solomon
SNG.writer: “The song of songs, which is Solomon's” (1:1). Tradition holds that Solomon wrote it.
SNG.when: If Solomon wrote it, about 950 BC.
SNG.to: Israel: a song for weddings, and for all who love.
SNG.why: To celebrate the love between a man and a woman as God's good gift.
SNG.summary: This is a love song: a bride and her bridegroom long for each other, seek each other and rejoice in each other. Jews read it as a picture of God's love for Israel, and Christians as a picture of Christ's love for His church. Its high point: “Love is as strong as death … Many waters cannot quench love” (8:6-7).
themes: Love between husband and wife is God's good gift.
Love is strong and faithful (8:6-7).
A picture of God's love for His people.
Do not stir up love before its time (2:7).
SNG.christ: The New Testament calls Christ the Bridegroom and the church His bride (Ephesians 5:25-32; Revelation 19:7). Many Christians have read the Song in this light.

ISA.title: The book of the prophet Isaiah
ISA.writer: Isaiah, son of Amoz, a prophet in Jerusalem (1:1). Many scholars think chapters 40–66 were written later by his followers; the New Testament quotes them under Isaiah's name (John 12:38-41).
ISA.when: Isaiah worked from about 740 to 680 BC, under four kings of Judah, while Assyria threatened the land.
ISA.to: Judah and Jerusalem, and through them the nations.
ISA.why: To call God's people to turn back, to warn of judgement, and to announce salvation through God's Servant.
ISA.summary: Isaiah sees the Lord on His throne: “Holy, holy, holy” (chapter 6). He warns Judah of judgement for its sin and injustice. He also announces a child, Immanuel, a King of David's line, and a time of peace. The second half comforts the people in exile: God will bring them home. It speaks of the Servant of the Lord, who suffers for the sins of others (chapter 53), and ends with new heavens and a new earth.
themes: God is the Holy One of Israel (6:3).
Judgement, and then comfort: “Comfort, yes, comfort My people” (40:1).
The Messiah: Immanuel, the Prince of Peace (7:14; 9:6).
The suffering Servant: “by His stripes we are healed” (53:5).
parts: Judgement and salvation for the world
Comfort: the Servant of the Lord
New heavens and a new earth
ISA.christ: Isaiah is called the gospel of the Old Testament. Jesus read from it in Nazareth: “Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:17-21). Chapter 53 describes His suffering and death for us (Acts 8:32-35).

JER.title: The book of the prophet Jeremiah
JER.line: Warning, tears and a new covenant
JER.writer: Jeremiah, a priest from Anathoth, who dictated his words to his scribe Baruch (36:4).
JER.when: Jeremiah worked from about 627 to 580 BC, through the last kings of Judah, the fall of Jerusalem (586 BC) and after.
JER.to: Judah and Jerusalem, and the exiles in Babylon.
JER.why: To call the people to turn back before it is too late, and to promise a new covenant after the judgement.
JER.summary: God calls Jeremiah as a young man. For forty years he warns that Babylon will come if the people do not turn back. They mock him, beat him and throw him into a pit. Jerusalem falls, as he said. Yet he also brings hope: God has thoughts of peace, to give a future and a hope (29:11), and He will make a new covenant and write His law on their hearts (31:31-34).
themes: A prophet called before he was born (1:5).
A changed heart, not empty religion (7:1-11).
God's thoughts of peace and hope (29:11).
The new covenant (31:31-34).
parts: Against false prophets; the letter to the exiles
The book of comfort: the new covenant
JER.christ: Jesus brought the new covenant that Jeremiah promised: “This cup is the new covenant in My blood” (Luke 22:20; Hebrews 8:8-12).

LAM.title: The Lamentations of Jeremiah
LAM.writer: The book does not name its writer. Tradition names Jeremiah, who saw Jerusalem fall.
LAM.when: Soon after Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and the temple in 586 BC.
LAM.why: To mourn the fall of the city before God, to confess sin, and to hold on to God's mercy.
LAM.summary: Five poems of grief over the ruined city. Four of them are alphabet poems: each verse begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. In the middle, in the darkest place, comes the great word of hope: “His compassions fail not. They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness” (3:22-23).
themes: Grief brought honestly before God.
Sin brings judgement (1:8).
God's mercies are new every morning (3:22-23).
Wait quietly for the salvation of the Lord (3:26).
LAM.christ: Jesus wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41). On the cross He bore the judgement, so that God's mercy is new for us every morning.

EZK.title: The book of the prophet Ezekiel
EZK.writer: Ezekiel, a priest who was taken to Babylon in 597 BC; he writes in his own words (1:1-3).
EZK.when: Ezekiel worked among the exiles in Babylon from about 593 to 571 BC.
EZK.to: The exiles in Babylon, and through them all Israel.
EZK.why: To show that God is present even in exile, to explain why Jerusalem fell, and to promise new life.
EZK.summary: By a river in Babylon, Ezekiel sees the glory of God: God is not bound to the temple. He sees the glory leave Jerusalem because of its sin, and the city falls. Then come words of hope: God will be their shepherd, give them a new heart and a new spirit, and make dry bones live. The book ends with a new temple, a river of life flowing from it, and a city whose name is “The Lord is there” (48:35).
themes: God's glory, present everywhere (chapter 1).
Each person answers for himself before God (chapter 18).
A new heart and a new spirit (36:26).
Dry bones live: God gives life (chapter 37).
parts: Hope: the shepherd, the new heart, the dry bones
The new temple and the river of life
EZK.christ: Jesus is the good shepherd Ezekiel promised (34:23; John 10:11). Through the Holy Spirit He gives the new heart and new life (John 3:5; 7:38-39).

DAN.title: The book of Daniel
DAN.writer: Daniel, taken to Babylon as a young man, as tradition holds; Jesus calls him “Daniel the prophet” (Matthew 24:15). Many scholars date the book to about 165 BC.
DAN.when: The stories cover Daniel's life in Babylon and Persia, from 605 to about 536 BC.
DAN.to: God's people living under foreign rulers.
DAN.why: To show that God rules over kings and kingdoms, and will set up a kingdom that lasts for ever.
DAN.summary: Daniel and his friends stay faithful to God at the court of Babylon. They refuse the king's food, the three friends survive the fiery furnace, and Daniel is kept safe in the lions' den. Daniel explains the king's dreams. In visions he sees kingdoms rise and fall, and “One like the Son of Man” who receives a kingdom that lasts for ever (7:13-14).
themes: Faithful in a foreign land (chapter 1).
God rules over the kingdoms of the world (4:17).
God saves those who trust Him (3:17-18; 6:22).
The Son of Man and the everlasting kingdom (7:13-14).
parts: Daniel and his friends in Babylon
Visions: the kingdoms and the Son of Man
DAN.christ: Jesus called Himself the Son of Man, and said He will come with the clouds of heaven (Mark 14:62; Daniel 7:13).

HOS.title: The book of the prophet Hosea
HOS.writer: Hosea, son of Beeri, a prophet in the northern kingdom (1:1).
HOS.when: About 755 to 715 BC, in the last years before Israel fell to Assyria.
HOS.why: To show that Israel's idolatry is like adultery, and that God's love still seeks His unfaithful people.
HOS.summary: God tells Hosea to marry Gomer, who is unfaithful to him. Their marriage becomes a picture of God and Israel: Israel runs after other gods, yet God's love will not let her go. Hosea buys his wife back, as God will heal and restore His people: “I will love them freely” (14:4).
themes: God's faithful love for an unfaithful people (11:8).
Idolatry is unfaithfulness to God.
I desire mercy and not sacrifice (6:6).
Return to the Lord, and He will heal (14:1-4).
parts: Hosea's marriage: a picture of God's love
Israel's unfaithfulness and the coming judgement
HOS.christ: “Out of Egypt I called My son” (11:1) is fulfilled in Jesus (Matthew 2:15). Jesus twice quoted “I desire mercy and not sacrifice” (Matthew 9:13; 12:7).

JOL.title: The book of the prophet Joel
JOL.line: The day of the Lord and the Spirit
JOL.writer: Joel, son of Pethuel (1:1). Nothing more is known of him.
JOL.when: Not known. Dates from about 830 BC to after the exile have been suggested.
JOL.why: To call the people to turn back after a plague of locusts, and to announce the day of the Lord and the outpouring of the Spirit.
JOL.summary: A terrible plague of locusts strips the land. Joel sees in it a warning of the coming day of the Lord. He calls everyone to fast and pray: “Rend your heart, and not your garments” (2:13). God promises to restore what the locusts have eaten, and to pour out His Spirit on all flesh.
themes: The day of the Lord (2:1).
Turning back with the whole heart (2:12-13).
God restores the lost years (2:25).
The Spirit poured out on all flesh (2:28-29).
parts: Return to the Lord; the Spirit promised
The nations judged; God's people restored
JOL.christ: On the day of Pentecost Peter said: this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel (Acts 2:16-21). The risen and exalted Christ poured out the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:33).

AMO.title: The book of the prophet Amos
AMO.writer: Amos, a shepherd and a grower of figs from Tekoa in Judah (1:1; 7:14).
AMO.when: About 760 BC, a time of wealth in the northern kingdom under King Jeroboam II.
AMO.why: To speak against injustice and empty worship, and to warn that God judges a people who oppress the poor.
AMO.summary: God sends a farmer from the south to the rich north. Amos speaks against those who live in luxury while the poor are trampled, and against worship without justice: “Let justice run down like water” (5:24). Israel will go into exile. Yet the book ends in hope: God will raise up the fallen tent of David.
themes: God cares about justice for the poor (2:6-7).
Worship without justice is empty (5:21-24).
Prepare to meet your God (4:12).
God will rebuild David's fallen tent (9:11).
parts: Judgement on the nations, and on Israel
AMO.christ: At the Apostles' council in Jerusalem, James quoted Amos 9:11-12: through Christ, God rebuilds David's house and gathers people from all nations (Acts 15:15-17).

OBA.title: The book of the prophet Obadiah
OBA.writer: Obadiah, whose name means “servant of the Lord”. Nothing more is known of him.
OBA.when: Most likely soon after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC.
OBA.why: To announce judgement on Edom, which rejoiced when Jerusalem fell, and the coming kingdom of the Lord.
OBA.summary: The shortest book of the Old Testament. Edom, which came from Esau, Jacob's brother, stood by and even helped when Jerusalem was destroyed. Obadiah announces that Edom's pride will bring it down: “As you have done, it shall be done to you” (verse 15). In the end, “the kingdom shall be the Lord's” (verse 21).
themes: Pride goes before a fall (verses 3-4).
God sees how we treat our brother in trouble (verses 10-14).
The kingdom shall be the Lord's (verse 21).
OBA.christ: The kingdom of the Lord that Obadiah announces comes in Jesus Christ, the King who humbled Himself and was exalted (Philippians 2:8-11).

JON.title: The book of the prophet Jonah
JON.writer: The story is about Jonah, son of Amittai, a prophet in the time of King Jeroboam II (2 Kings 14:25). The writer is not named.
JON.when: The story happens about 760 BC. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria, Israel's enemy.
JON.to: Israel, to see God's mercy for the nations.
JON.why: To show that God's mercy reaches even Israel's enemies, and to challenge a narrow heart.
JON.summary: God sends Jonah to warn Nineveh. Jonah flees by ship, is thrown into the sea and swallowed by a great fish. He prays, and God saves him. Then he preaches in Nineveh, and the whole city repents. God spares it. Jonah is angry, and God asks him: should I not pity this great city? (4:11).
themes: You cannot run away from God (chapter 1).
Salvation is of the Lord (2:9).
God's mercy for all people, even for enemies (3:10).
God's heart is bigger than ours (4:10-11).
JON.christ: Jesus spoke of the sign of Jonah: as Jonah was three days and three nights in the fish, so the Son of Man would be three days in the heart of the earth, and rise (Matthew 12:39-41).

MIC.title: The book of the prophet Micah
MIC.writer: Micah of Moresheth, a country town in Judah (1:1). He was a prophet at the same time as Isaiah.
MIC.when: About 735 to 700 BC, under the kings Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah.
MIC.why: To expose injustice and false prophets, to warn of judgement, and to promise a ruler from Bethlehem.
MIC.summary: Micah speaks against leaders who abuse the poor, and prophets who preach for money. Jerusalem will fall. Yet God will gather His people, and a ruler will come from little Bethlehem, who will shepherd them in the strength of the Lord (5:2-4). God asks only this: “to do justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God” (6:8).
themes: Do justly, love mercy, walk humbly (6:8).
A ruler from Bethlehem (5:2).
Swords into ploughshares: God's coming peace (4:3).
Who is a God like You, who pardons sin? (7:18).
parts: False leaders; the ruler from Bethlehem
God's case against His people; His mercy
MIC.christ: When the wise men asked where the Christ would be born, the scribes answered with Micah 5:2: in Bethlehem (Matthew 2:4-6).

NAM.title: The book of the prophet Nahum
NAM.writer: Nahum the Elkoshite (1:1). His name means “comfort”.
NAM.when: Between the fall of Thebes in Egypt (663 BC, named in 3:8) and the fall of Nineveh (612 BC).
NAM.why: To comfort God's people: the cruel empire of Assyria will fall.
NAM.summary: About a hundred years after Jonah, Nineveh is again full of violence and cruelty. Nahum announces its fall. God is slow to anger, but He will not leave the guilty unpunished. For Judah this is good news: “The Lord is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble” (1:7). Nineveh fell in 612 BC.
themes: God is patient, but He judges evil (1:3).
The Lord is good, a refuge in trouble (1:7).
Good news of peace (1:15).
parts: The Lord is jealous, and good
NAM.christ: “The feet of him who brings good tidings” (1:15) is taken up by Paul for those who preach the gospel of Christ (Romans 10:15).

HAB.title: The book of the prophet Habakkuk
HAB.writer: Habakkuk the prophet (1:1). Nothing more is known of him.
HAB.when: About 605 BC, just before Babylon invaded Judah.
HAB.to: Judah, and all who wonder why God allows evil.
HAB.why: To wrestle with God about evil and injustice, and to learn to trust Him.
HAB.summary: Habakkuk asks God: why do You let evil go on? God answers: I am sending Babylon to judge Judah. Habakkuk asks again: how can You use people more wicked than us? God answers: the proud will fall, “but the just shall live by his faith” (2:4). The book ends with a prayer of trust: though the fig tree does not blossom, “yet I will rejoice in the Lord” (3:17-18).
themes: Honest questions to God (1:2-4).
The just shall live by faith (2:4).
The earth will be filled with the knowledge of God's glory (2:14).
Joy in God when everything fails (3:17-19).
parts: The first question and God's answer
The second question; the just shall live by faith
HAB.christ: “The just shall live by faith” is quoted three times in the New Testament (Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11; Hebrews 10:38): we are made right with God by faith in Jesus Christ.

ZEP.title: The book of the prophet Zephaniah
ZEP.line: The day of the Lord; God's joy
ZEP.writer: Zephaniah, a great-great-grandson of King Hezekiah (1:1).
ZEP.when: About 630 BC, under King Josiah, probably before his reforms.
ZEP.why: To warn of the day of the Lord, to call to humility, and to promise joy for the humble.
ZEP.summary: Zephaniah announces the great day of the Lord, a day of judgement on Judah and the nations. He calls: “Seek the Lord, all you meek of the earth” (2:3). After the judgement God will keep a humble people. The book ends in great joy: God rejoices over His people with singing (3:17).
themes: The great day of the Lord is near (1:14).
Seek the Lord, seek humility (2:3).
God keeps a humble remnant (3:12).
God rejoices over you with singing (3:17).
parts: Seek the Lord; the nations judged
Jerusalem judged and restored; God's joy
ZEP.christ: “The King of Israel, the Lord, is in your midst” (3:15). This is fulfilled in Jesus, who came to live among His people.

HAG.title: The book of the prophet Haggai
HAG.writer: Haggai the prophet (1:1). He worked together with Zechariah (Ezra 5:1).
HAG.when: In 520 BC: four messages in four months, eighteen years after the first return from exile.
HAG.to: Zerubbabel the governor, Joshua the high priest, and the returned exiles.
HAG.why: To stir the people to finish rebuilding the temple.
HAG.summary: The returned exiles have built their own houses, but the temple still lies in ruins. Haggai says: “Consider your ways” (1:5). They work hard but have little, because God's house is neglected. The people listen and begin to build. God encourages them: “I am with you” (1:13), and the glory of this house will be greater than the former (2:9).
themes: Put God's house first (1:4-9).
Consider your ways (1:5).
Be strong and work, for I am with you (2:4).
God's coming glory and peace (2:9).
parts: Build the house of the Lord
Its glory will be greater; God's promise to Zerubbabel
HAG.christ: The greater glory of the temple came when the Lord Jesus Christ Himself came into it (Malachi 3:1; Luke 2:27-32).

ZEC.title: The book of the prophet Zechariah
ZEC.writer: Zechariah, son of Berechiah, a priest and prophet (1:1). Many scholars think chapters 9–14 were added later.
ZEC.when: From 520 BC, at the same time as Haggai, while the temple was being rebuilt.
ZEC.why: To encourage the people to build and to return to God, and to show the King who is coming.
ZEC.summary: Zechariah calls: “Return to Me, and I will return to you” (1:3). In eight night visions he sees God's care for Jerusalem and its leaders: “Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit” (4:6). The second half speaks of the coming King, humble and riding on a donkey (9:9), of the shepherd who is struck (13:7), and of the day when the Lord will be King over all the earth (14:9).
themes: Return to God (1:3).
Not by might but by God's Spirit (4:6).
The humble King (9:9).
They will look on Him whom they pierced (12:10).
parts: The coming King and the day of the Lord
ZEC.christ: Zechariah is quoted many times in the account of Jesus' last week: the King on a donkey (Matthew 21:5), the thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 27:9-10), the shepherd struck (Matthew 26:31) and the One they pierced (John 19:37).

MAL.title: The book of the prophet Malachi
MAL.when: About 430 BC, around the time of Nehemiah. He is the last prophet of the Old Testament.
MAL.to: The people of Judah after the return, grown careless in their faith.
MAL.why: To call the people and the priests back to wholehearted worship, and to announce the coming messenger and the day of the Lord.
MAL.summary: The temple stands again, but faith has grown cold. Malachi puts God's questions to the people: they offer poor sacrifices, are unfaithful in marriage, and rob God in tithes and offerings. God says: “I have loved you” (1:2) and “Return to Me” (3:7). He will send His messenger to prepare the way, and the Lord will come to His temple. The Old Testament ends with the promise of Elijah before the great day.
themes: God's love for His people (1:2).
Give God your best (1:6-14).
Return to Me, and I will return to you (3:7).
The messenger who prepares the way (3:1; 4:5-6).
parts: Priests and people who dishonour God
The messenger, the tithes and the day of the Lord
MAL.christ: Jesus said that John the Baptist is the messenger Malachi foretold, the Elijah who was to come (Matthew 11:10-14). Then the Lord came to His temple.

1ES.title: The first book of Esdras
1ES.writer: The writer is not named. The book retells parts of 2 Chronicles, Ezra and Nehemiah in Greek, with one story of its own.
1ES.when: Written about 150 BC. It tells of King Josiah's Passover (about 622 BC) up to Ezra reading the law (about 445 BC).
1ES.why: To tell again how the temple and its worship were restored after the exile, and to honour the truth.
1ES.summary: 1 Esdras retells the last kings of Judah, the exile, the return under Zerubbabel, the rebuilding of the temple and Ezra's reform. Its own story is the contest of three young guards before King Darius: what is strongest, wine, the king, or women? Zerubbabel answers: truth is strongest of all. “Great is Truth, and mighty above all things” (4:41).
themes: God restores His people after the exile.
Worship rightly ordered (chapters 1 and 7).
The truth endures and is always strong (4:38).
parts: The three guards: truth is strongest
1ES.christ: Jesus said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). The truth that is stronger than all is fully revealed in Him.

2ES.title: The second book of Esdras
2ES.writer: Written in the name of Ezra. The heart of the book (chapters 3–14) is a Jewish writing; chapters 1–2 and 15–16 were added later by Christians.
2ES.when: Chapters 3–14 are usually dated about AD 100, after the Romans destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70; the added chapters are later still. So it is younger than the other later writings, which the Catechism places between the third and the first century BC (CNAC 1.2.3).
2ES.to: God's people grieving over the fall of Jerusalem.
2ES.why: To wrestle with the question why God lets His people suffer, and to point to the end of this age and the world to come.
2ES.summary: In seven visions Ezra argues with the angel Uriel: why has Zion fallen, while those who wronged her prosper? He learns that God's ways are beyond our understanding, that this age will pass, and that a new age is coming for those who stay faithful. He sees a mourning woman become a shining city, and the Messiah rising from the sea.
themes: Honest questions in grief (chapter 3).
God's ways are beyond our understanding (4:1-11).
This age passes; the world to come.
The Messiah and the judgement (chapters 7 and 13).
parts: A Christian opening: God's people called
A Christian ending: warnings and comfort
2ES.christ: The Christian chapters speak of the Son of God whom the faithful have confessed in the world (2:47), and of the Shepherd who gives everlasting rest (2:34). The longing for the end of the age is answered by Christ's promise to come again.

TOB.title: The book of Tobit
TOB.writer: The writer is not named. The first chapters are told in Tobit's own words.
TOB.when: Written about 200 BC. The story is set among the exiles in Nineveh, after 722 BC.
TOB.why: To show that God cares for those who stay faithful in a foreign land, in prayer, in giving to the poor, and in love for their family.
TOB.summary: Tobit, a devout man in exile, buries the dead and gives alms, yet he becomes blind. Far away, a young woman, Sarah, suffers too. Both pray on the same day, and God hears them. Tobit sends his son Tobias on a journey, and the angel Raphael goes with him, unrecognised. Tobias marries Sarah, and Tobit's sight is restored. Then Raphael tells who he is and says: give thanks to God.
themes: God hears the prayers of the troubled (3:16).
Giving to the poor and doing good (4:7-11; 12:8-9).
Angels serve God's people (12:15).
Honour your father and mother; be faithful in the family (chapter 4).
parts: Tobit and Sarah in trouble; their prayers
Raphael revealed; Tobit's song and last words
TOB.christ: Tobit says: “Do that to no man which thou hatest” (4:15). Jesus says it the other way round: do to others what you would have them do to you (Matthew 7:12). God's care for the exiles points to the Good Shepherd, who seeks the lost.

JDT.title: The book of Judith
JDT.when: Written about 150 to 100 BC. The story mixes names and times from different centuries, which suggests it was told as a lesson more than as a history.
JDT.to: Jews under the threat of foreign powers.
JDT.why: To show that God saves His people through faith and courage, even through a woman when the men lose heart.
JDT.summary: The general Holofernes besieges the town of Bethulia, and its leaders are ready to give up within five days. Judith, a devout widow, rebukes them: do not bind the counsels of the Lord (8:16). She prays, goes into the enemy camp, and beheads Holofernes while he lies drunk. The army flees, and Israel sings God's praise.
themes: Do not set God a deadline (8:11-17).
Prayer before action (chapter 9).
God is the God of the lowly and the helper of the oppressed (9:11).
Praise after deliverance (chapter 16).
parts: Judith rebukes the elders and prays
Judith in the camp of Holofernes
JDT.christ: Judith praises the God of the lowly (9:11). Mary's song praises the same God, who has put down the mighty and lifted up the lowly (Luke 1:52).

ESG.title: The rest of the chapters of the book of Esther
ESG.writer: The writer is not named. The additions come from the Greek translation of Esther, which a note at its end dates to about 114 BC (11:1).
ESG.when: Added in the second or first century BC to the Greek version of Esther.
ESG.to: Jews who read Esther in Greek.
ESG.why: To bring out what the Hebrew book of Esther leaves unsaid: that God is the One who saves, and that Esther and Mordecai prayed.
ESG.summary: Six additions to the book of Esther, gathered in the King James Bible as chapters 10 to 16. They tell Mordecai's dream and its meaning, give the text of the king's letters, and set down the prayers of Mordecai and Esther before Esther goes in to the king. Here God's name is spoken many times.
themes: God is the One who saves His people (10:9).
Prayer before a dangerous step (chapters 13–14).
God remembered His people (10:12).
parts: The king's letter; the prayers of Mordecai and Esther
Esther before the king; the second letter
ESG.christ: Esther prays: “O my Lord, thou only art our King” (14:3). This points to Christ, the King who saves His people.

WIS.title: The Wisdom of Solomon
WIS.writer: Written in Solomon's name by a Jewish teacher, most likely in Alexandria in Egypt, in Greek.
WIS.when: Most likely in the first century BC.
WIS.to: Jews living among Greeks, tempted by their wisdom and their idols.
WIS.why: To show that true wisdom comes from God, that the righteous have hope beyond death, and that idols are empty.
WIS.summary: The book speaks to rulers and to all: love righteousness and seek God. “The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God” (3:1); the ungodly think life ends at death, but they are wrong. Then Solomon praises wisdom as “the brightness of the everlasting light” (7:26) and asks God for her in prayer. The last part retells the exodus, to show God's care for His people and the folly of idols.
themes: The souls of the righteous are in God's hand (3:1).
Wisdom is a gift of God; pray for it (chapter 9).
God loves all that He has made (11:24).
Idols are empty; God alone is to be worshipped (chapters 13–15).
parts: Righteousness and the hope of eternal life
Solomon praises wisdom and prays for it
Wisdom in history: the exodus and the folly of idols
WIS.christ: The New Testament speaks of Christ in words close to this book: He is the brightness of God's glory and the express image of His person (Hebrews 1:3; compare 7:26).

SIR.title: The Wisdom of Jesus the son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
SIR.writer: Jesus (Joshua) son of Sirach, a teacher in Jerusalem (50:27). His grandson translated it into Greek in Egypt and wrote a foreword.
SIR.when: Written about 180 BC; translated about 132 BC.
SIR.to: Young people, and all who want to live wisely by God's law.
SIR.why: To teach wisdom for daily life, rooted in the fear of the Lord and the law of Moses.
SIR.summary: Ecclesiasticus is the longest wisdom book: short teachings on friendship, speech, work, money, family, health and prayer. Wisdom comes from the Lord and lives in His law. The book ends with the “praise of famous men” (chapters 44–50), from Enoch to the high priest Simon, and a prayer of thanks.
themes: All wisdom comes from the Lord (1:1).
The fear of the Lord is honour, glory and gladness (1:11).
Prepare for testing when you serve the Lord (2:1-6).
Remember the faithful who went before us (44:1).
parts: More teaching; God's works in creation
A prayer of thanks; seek wisdom
SIR.christ: Jesus' invitation, “Come to Me … take My yoke upon you” (Matthew 11:28-30), is close to Sirach's call to come to wisdom and put your neck under her yoke (51:23-26). In Christ, God's wisdom has come in person.

BAR.title: The book of Baruch, with the Epistle of Jeremiah
BAR.writer: Named after Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe (1:1). Most scholars think it was written later in his name. Chapter 6 is a letter in Jeremiah's name.
BAR.when: Set in the exile in Babylon, about 582 BC; most likely written between 200 and 100 BC.
BAR.to: The exiles in Babylon, and the people in Jerusalem.
BAR.why: To lead the people to confession, to point them to God's wisdom in His law, and to comfort them with the hope of return.
BAR.summary: The exiles confess their sins in a long prayer: “To the Lord our God belongeth righteousness, but unto us the confusion of faces” (1:15). Then a poem praises wisdom, which God gave to Israel in the law. A third part comforts Jerusalem: her children will come home. Chapter 6, the letter of Jeremiah, warns against the idols of Babylon.
themes: Honest confession of sin (1:15–3:8).
Wisdom is found in God's law (3:9–4:4).
Take courage: God will bring His people home (4:21-30).
Idols are powerless (chapter 6).
parts: Wisdom in the law; comfort for Jerusalem
The letter of Jeremiah against idols
BAR.christ: Of wisdom, Baruch says: “Afterward did he shew himself upon earth, and conversed with men” (3:37). The early church read this as pointing to the Word made flesh, who lived among us (John 1:14).

S3Y.title: The Song of the Three Holy Children
S3Y.writer: The writer is not named. It is an addition to Daniel 3 in the Greek Bible.
S3Y.when: Most likely written in the second century BC.
S3Y.to: God's people, to praise God in trial.
S3Y.why: To give the prayer and the song of the three young men in the fiery furnace.
S3Y.summary: In the furnace, Azarias (Abednego) prays, confessing Israel's sins and asking for mercy. The angel of the Lord comes down and drives the flame out of the furnace. Then the three young men sing a great song of praise, calling all creation to bless the Lord: “O all ye works of the Lord, bless ye the Lord” (verse 35). The church has sung it for centuries as the “Benedicite”.
themes: Prayer and confession in the fire (verses 3-22).
God is with His people in trial (verse 26).
All creation, bless the Lord (verses 35-66).
S3Y.christ: In the furnace was a fourth man, “like the Son of God” (Daniel 3:25), and the angel drove out the flame. God is with His people in the fire, as Christ promises: “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20).

SUS.title: The history of Susanna
SUS.writer: The writer is not named. It is an addition to Daniel in the Greek Bible.
SUS.when: Most likely written in the second or first century BC; the story is set in Babylon in the exile.
SUS.to: God's people, about justice and trust.
SUS.why: To show that God protects the innocent who trust Him, and exposes false witnesses.
SUS.summary: Two elders, who are also judges, lust after Susanna, a faithful wife. When she refuses them, they accuse her falsely, and she is condemned to death. She cries out to God. Young Daniel stands up, questions the two elders apart, and their lies come out: they name different trees. Susanna is saved, and the false witnesses are punished.
themes: Rather suffer than sin before the Lord (verse 23).
God hears the cry of the innocent (verses 42-44).
Justice: test the witnesses (verses 51-59).
God saves those who trust in Him (verse 60).
SUS.christ: Like Susanna, Jesus was condemned on the word of false witnesses (Matthew 26:59-61). God set Him right by raising Him from the dead.

BEL.title: Bel and the Dragon
BEL.writer: The writer is not named. It is an addition to Daniel in the Greek Bible.
BEL.when: Most likely written in the second or first century BC; the story is set in Babylon under King Cyrus.
BEL.to: God's people living among people who worship idols.
BEL.why: To show that idols are not living gods, and that the living God protects His servant.
BEL.summary: Two stories. In the first, Daniel shows the king that the idol Bel does not eat the food set before it: the priests and their families do, through a secret door. In the second, Daniel kills a dragon the Babylonians worship, and is thrown into the lions' den. The prophet Habakkuk is carried there to feed him, and on the seventh day the king finds Daniel alive.
themes: Idols are made by hands; God is living (verse 5).
A wise faith exposes lies.
God feeds and protects His servant (verses 33-39).
BEL.christ: The living God whom Daniel worships is revealed in Jesus Christ, the Living One, who was dead and is alive for evermore (Revelation 1:18).

MAN.title: The Prayer of Manasses, king of Judah
MAN.writer: Written in the name of King Manasseh, who repented when he was a captive (2 Chronicles 33:12-13, 18-19).
MAN.when: Most likely written in the second or first century BC.
MAN.to: Every sinner who wants to come back to God.
MAN.why: To give words of repentance to someone who has done great evil, and to show God's mercy.
MAN.summary: Manasseh was one of the worst kings of Judah. In captivity he humbled himself, and God heard him. This short prayer gives his words: he praises God's power and His endless mercy, confesses his many sins, and asks for forgiveness: “I bow the knee of mine heart, beseeching thee of grace.”
themes: God's mercy is greater than our sin.
Repentance from the heart.
God is the God of those who repent.
MAN.christ: Jesus came to call sinners to repentance (Luke 5:32), and there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:7).

1MA.title: The first book of the Maccabees
1MA.writer: The writer is not named: a Jew in Judea who knew the Maccabees well, writing in Hebrew.
1MA.when: Written about 100 BC. It tells of the years 175 to 134 BC.
1MA.why: To tell how God saved His people when a foreign king tried to stamp out their faith, and how they won back their freedom and the temple.
1MA.summary: The Greek king Antiochus IV forbids Jewish worship and defiles the temple. The priest Mattathias and his sons refuse to obey and rise up. Judas Maccabeus (“the hammer”) wins great battles, cleanses the temple and dedicates it again; this is remembered in the feast of dedication, Hanukkah (John 10:22). His brothers Jonathan and Simon carry on the fight and lead the people.
themes: Faithful to God when faith is forbidden (2:21).
Victory comes from heaven, not from numbers (3:18-19).
The temple cleansed and dedicated (4:36-59).
God helps His people.
1MA.christ: Jesus was in the temple at the feast of dedication (John 10:22-23), which remembers 1 Maccabees 4. He Himself is the true temple (John 2:19-21).

2MA.title: The second book of the Maccabees
2MA.writer: A summary, by a writer who is not named, of a history in five books by Jason of Cyrene (2:23), in Greek.
2MA.when: Written about 124 BC or somewhat later. It tells of the years from about 180 to 161 BC.
2MA.to: The Jews in Egypt, invited to keep the feast of the cleansing of the temple.
2MA.why: To show God's care for the temple and His people, and to encourage faithfulness to death in the hope of the resurrection.
2MA.summary: 2 Maccabees tells some of the same history as 1 Maccabees, with more about the martyrs. The old scribe Eleazar dies rather than eat pork. A mother and her seven sons are put to death, confessing that God will raise them up (chapter 7). Judas wins his battles by prayer. After a battle he has a sin offering made for the fallen, because he believes they will rise again (12:43-45).
themes: Faithful to death: the martyrs (chapters 6–7).
The hope of the resurrection (7:9; 12:43-44).
God made all things out of nothing (7:28).
Prayer and offering for the departed (12:43-45).
2MA.christ: The hope of the resurrection that the martyrs confess is fulfilled in Jesus Christ, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Corinthians 15:20).

MAT.title: The Gospel according to Matthew
MAT.writer: Matthew, also called Levi, the tax collector whom Jesus called to follow Him (9:9). The early church named him as the writer; the book itself does not give a name.
MAT.when: Most scholars date it between AD 60 and 80. It tells of Jesus' life from His birth (about 6–4 BC) to His resurrection (about AD 30).
MAT.to: Jewish Christians first, who knew the Old Testament well, and through them the whole church.
MAT.why: To show that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of David promised in the Old Testament, and to teach His followers how to live in the kingdom of heaven.
MAT.summary: Matthew opens with Jesus' family line from Abraham and David, and again and again he says: this happened to fulfil what the prophets said. Jesus teaches in five long speeches; the first is the Sermon on the Mount. He heals, calls His disciples and meets growing opposition. In Jerusalem He is crucified, and He rises again. The book ends with the risen Lord sending His Apostles to all nations: “I am with you always, to the end of the age” (28:20).
themes: Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of David, who fulfils the Scriptures (1:1; 5:17).
The kingdom of heaven has come near (4:17).
Living as Jesus' disciple: the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5–7).
The church that Christ builds (16:18) and sends to all nations (28:19).
parts: Jesus' birth and the start of His work
Jesus in Galilee: miracles, parables and the disciples
On the way to Jerusalem; teaching on the end
MAT.christ: Matthew calls Jesus “Immanuel, God with us” (1:23), and ends with His promise: “I am with you always” (28:20). Jesus is the King in David's line, the Teacher greater than Moses, and the Son of the living God (16:16).

MRK.title: The Gospel according to Mark
MRK.line: Jesus, the Servant Son of God
MRK.writer: John Mark from Jerusalem, who travelled with Paul and Barnabas (Acts 12:25) and later with Peter (1 Peter 5:13). Early church writers say he wrote down what Peter preached.
MRK.when: About AD 65–70, probably in Rome. After Paul's letters, Mark is the oldest written witness of the Christian faith; Matthew and Luke are closely related to it (CNAC 1.2.4.1).
MRK.to: Christians who were not Jews, probably in Rome: Mark explains Jewish customs (7:3-4) and Aramaic words (5:41).
MRK.why: To tell “the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God” (1:1) quickly and plainly: who He is, and that His way led through the cross.
MRK.summary: Mark is the shortest gospel, and it moves fast: the word “immediately” comes again and again. Jesus preaches, heals and casts out demons with authority. Halfway through, Peter confesses: “You are the Christ” (8:29). From then on Jesus tells His disciples three times that He must suffer, die and rise again. At the cross a Roman officer says: “Truly this Man was the Son of God!” (15:39). The women find the tomb empty.
themes: Jesus acts with God's authority over sickness, demons, the storm and sin (2:10; 4:41).
Who is Jesus? The question runs through the book (8:29).
The Son of Man came to serve and to give His life (10:45).
Following Jesus means taking up the cross (8:34).
parts: On the way: Jesus speaks of His suffering
In Jerusalem: the cross and the empty tomb
MRK.christ: Mark shows Jesus as the Servant who came “to give His life a ransom for many” (10:45). The Son of God is seen most clearly at the cross (15:39).

LUK.title: The Gospel according to Luke
LUK.writer: Luke, “the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14), a companion of Paul. He also wrote Acts (Acts 1:1). He was probably not a Jew, and he says he looked carefully into everything from the start (1:3).
LUK.to: Theophilus (1:3), probably a man of rank who had been taught about Jesus, and through him all who are not Jews.
LUK.why: To give an orderly account, so that the reader may be sure of the things he was taught (1:4).
LUK.summary: Luke tells the most about Jesus' birth and childhood: the angel and Mary, the shepherds, the boy Jesus in the temple. Jesus begins His work in Nazareth with the words of Isaiah: good news to the poor, freedom for the captives (4:18). Then comes a long journey to Jerusalem (9:51), full of parables found only in Luke: the good Samaritan, the lost sheep, the lost son. Jesus makes time for the poor, for women, for sinners and for outsiders. After the resurrection He walks with two disciples to Emmaus and opens the Scriptures to them.
themes: Jesus came to seek and to save the lost (19:10).
Good news for the poor, the outsider and the sinner (4:18; 15:1-2).
Prayer: Jesus prays at every turning point (3:21; 6:12; 22:41).
The Holy Spirit and joy (1:35; 2:10; 10:21).
parts: In Jerusalem: the cross, the empty tomb, Emmaus
LUK.christ: Luke shows Jesus as the Saviour of all people (2:11, 32). On the road to Emmaus the risen Lord shows that Moses and all the prophets speak of Him (24:27).

JHN.title: The Gospel according to John
JHN.writer: John, the son of Zebedee, one of the Twelve. The early church held that he is “the disciple whom Jesus loved”, who wrote this gospel (21:20-24).
JHN.when: About AD 85–95, probably in Ephesus. Most scholars think it is the last of the four gospels.
JHN.to: Believers and seekers everywhere, so that they may believe (20:31).
JHN.why: “That you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in His name” (20:31).
JHN.summary: John begins before creation: “In the beginning was the Word… and the Word was God” (1:1), and that Word became a human being (1:14). John tells of seven signs, from water turned into wine to Lazarus raised from the dead, and of Jesus' “I am” sayings: the bread of life, the light of the world, the good shepherd, the resurrection and the life. On the last evening Jesus washes His disciples' feet, promises to come again and to send the Holy Spirit, the Helper, and prays for all who will believe (chapters 13–17). Then come the cross, the empty tomb, and the risen Lord with Mary, Thomas and Peter.
themes: Jesus is God's Son, one with the Father (10:30).
Believe and live: eternal life begins now (3:16; 5:24).
The Holy Spirit, the Helper, sent to the disciples (14:26; 16:13).
“I will come again and receive you to Myself” (14:3).
Love one another, as I have loved you (13:34).
parts: The signs: Jesus shows who He is
The last evening with His disciples
JHN.christ: John shows Jesus as the eternal Word who was God and became flesh (1:1, 14). His “I am” sayings echo God's own name (Exodus 3:14), and Thomas confesses: “My Lord and my God!” (20:28).

ACT.title: The Acts of the Apostles
ACT.writer: Luke the physician, who also wrote the Gospel of Luke (1:1). In some passages he says “we”: he travelled with Paul (16:10).
ACT.when: It tells of the time from Jesus' ascension (about AD 30) to Paul in Rome (about AD 62), and was probably written soon after, about AD 62–80.
ACT.to: Theophilus again (1:1), and the whole church.
ACT.why: To show how the risen Lord, through the Holy Spirit and His Apostles, spread the gospel from Jerusalem to Rome.
ACT.summary: Acts begins where Luke ends: Jesus ascends to heaven, and the angels say He will come again in the same way (1:11). At Pentecost the Holy Spirit is poured out, Peter preaches, and about three thousand are baptised. The first congregation continues in the Apostles' doctrine, in fellowship, in the breaking of bread and in prayer (2:42). Stephen dies as the first martyr. In Samaria, people who were baptised with water receive the Holy Spirit when the Apostles Peter and John lay their hands on them (8:14-17). Saul, who persecuted the church, meets the risen Lord and becomes Paul, the Apostle to the nations. The book follows his journeys and ends with him preaching in Rome.
themes: The Holy Spirit is the power behind the church's growth (1:8; 2:4).
The Apostles lead the church, and through the laying on of their hands the Holy Spirit is given (8:14-17; 19:6). The Catechism finds Holy Sealing here (CNAC 8.3.5).
The gospel is for all nations: Jews, Samaritans and gentiles (10:34-35).
There is salvation in no one else but Jesus (4:12).
parts: Paul a prisoner, on the way to Rome
ACT.christ: Acts carries on what Jesus “began both to do and teach” (1:1): the risen and ascended Lord keeps working through His Apostles and the Holy Spirit. And the angels promise: this same Jesus will come again (1:11).

ROM.title: The letter of Paul to the Romans
ROM.writer: The Apostle Paul (1:1). He spoke the letter to a helper, Tertius, who wrote it down (16:22).
ROM.when: About AD 57, from Corinth, near the end of Paul's third journey.
ROM.to: The congregation in Rome, of Jewish and gentile believers, which Paul had not yet visited (1:10-13).
ROM.why: To set out the gospel he preached, to bring Jewish and gentile believers together, and to prepare for his visit on the way to Spain (15:24).
ROM.summary: Romans is Paul's fullest teaching on the gospel. All people, Jews and gentiles, have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (3:23). But God makes people right with Himself freely, by His grace, through faith in Jesus Christ, who died for us while we were still sinners (3:24; 5:8). In baptism we died with Christ to sin and were raised to a new life (6:4). The Holy Spirit lives in us and makes us God's children (8:14-16), and nothing can separate us from God's love (8:38-39). Paul wrestles with Israel's place in God's plan (chapters 9–11), and ends with how to live: as a living sacrifice, in love, and in peace with one another.
themes: All have sinned; no one is made right with God by their own works (3:23).
Made right with God by grace, through faith (3:24; 5:1).
A new life in Christ and in the Holy Spirit (6:4; 8:1-17).
God's faithfulness to Israel and to the nations (chapters 9–11).
Living as a living sacrifice (12:1-2).
parts: Made right with God through faith
New life in Christ and in the Spirit
Israel and the nations in God's plan
ROM.christ: At the heart of Romans stands Christ, who died for us and rose again; for those who are in Him there is now no condemnation (8:1). Through the obedience of the one man Jesus Christ many are made righteous (5:19).

1CO.title: The first letter of Paul to the Corinthians
1CO.writer: The Apostle Paul, together with Sosthenes (1:1).
1CO.to: The congregation in Corinth, a rich and busy port city in Greece, which Paul had founded (Acts 18).
1CO.why: To answer the congregation's questions and to put right what had gone wrong: quarrels, pride, sin, disorder in the divine service and doubts about the resurrection.
1CO.summary: The congregation in Corinth was gifted but divided: some followed Paul, others Apollos or Peter (1:12). Paul points them to Christ crucified, who is God's power and God's wisdom (1:18-24). He deals with sin in the congregation, with marriage, with food offered to idols and with order in the divine service. He hands on what he received from the Lord about Holy Communion (11:23-26). He speaks of the gifts of the Spirit and the one body with many members (chapter 12), and then shows the most excellent way: love (chapter 13). Chapter 15 is the great chapter on the resurrection: Christ is risen, and at the last trumpet the dead will be raised and we shall be changed (15:51-52).
themes: The message of the cross: God's wisdom, foolishness to the world (1:18).
One body, many members, one Spirit (12:12-13).
Love is the greatest (13:13).
Holy Communion: we proclaim the Lord's death till He comes (11:26).
Christ is risen, and so shall we be (15:20). The congregation in Corinth was even baptised for the dead (15:29); the Catechism refers to this for the divine services for the departed (CNAC 12.1.13).
parts: Divisions, and the message of the cross
Sin in the congregation, and marriage
Freedom and love: food offered to idols
The divine service: Holy Communion, gifts and love
1CO.christ: Paul preaches “Jesus Christ and Him crucified” (2:2). Christ is the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (15:20): His resurrection is the promise of ours, at His coming (15:23).

2CO.title: The second letter of Paul to the Corinthians
2CO.writer: The Apostle Paul, together with Timothy (1:1).
2CO.when: About AD 55–56, from Macedonia (7:5), on Paul's third journey.
2CO.to: The congregation in Corinth and all the believers in Achaia, in Greece (1:1).
2CO.why: To make peace after a painful time, to defend his ministry as an Apostle against those who looked down on him, and to encourage a gift for the poor in Jerusalem.
2CO.summary: This is Paul's most personal letter. He tells of his suffering and of God's comfort (1:3-4). He describes the ministry of the new covenant: “we have this treasure in earthen vessels” (4:7). Whoever is in Christ is a new creation (5:17), and God has given His messengers the ministry of reconciliation: “we implore you on Christ's behalf, be reconciled to God” (5:20). Chapters 8 and 9 ask for a generous gift for the poor. In chapters 10 to 13 Paul defends his apostleship and tells of his “thorn in the flesh”, and of the Lord's answer: “My grace is sufficient for you, for My strength is made perfect in weakness” (12:9).
themes: God comforts us so that we can comfort others (1:3-4).
The ministry of reconciliation: God reconciles the world to Himself in Christ (5:18-20).
A new creation in Christ (5:17).
Cheerful giving (9:7).
God's strength is made perfect in weakness (12:9).
2CO.christ: God made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in Him (5:21). The Apostles are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were pleading through them (5:20).

GAL.title: The letter of Paul to the Galatians
GAL.writer: The Apostle Paul (1:1). He wrote the end with his own hand, in large letters (6:11).
GAL.when: About AD 49–55. Scholars differ on whether it is one of Paul's first letters or was written some years later.
GAL.to: The congregations in Galatia, in what is now Turkey.
GAL.why: Teachers had come who said that gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. Paul writes that we are made right with God by grace, through faith in Christ, and not by the works of the law.
GAL.summary: Paul is upset: the Galatians are turning to “a different gospel” (1:6). He tells how he received the gospel from the risen Lord, and how the Apostles in Jerusalem recognised his calling (chapters 1 and 2). Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness (3:6); the law was a tutor to bring us to Christ (3:24). In Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female (3:28). Christ has set us free (5:1), but freedom is not an excuse to sin: walk in the Spirit, and the fruit of the Spirit will grow (5:22-23).
themes: Made right with God by faith in Christ, not by the works of the law (2:16).
All one in Christ Jesus (3:28).
Freedom in Christ (5:1).
The fruit of the Spirit (5:22-23).
GAL.christ: “I have been crucified with Christ; it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (2:20). Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (3:13).

EPH.title: The letter of Paul to the Ephesians
EPH.writer: The Apostle Paul (1:1), writing as a prisoner (3:1; 4:1). Some scholars think a pupil wrote it in his name.
EPH.when: About AD 60–62, probably from prison in Rome.
EPH.to: The believers in Ephesus, and probably other congregations in the area too: some old copies leave out the words “in Ephesus”.
EPH.why: To show God's great plan to bring all things together in Christ and the place of the church in it, and to call believers to live up to their calling.
EPH.summary: Ephesians begins with praise: God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world, and we were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise (1:3-14). We are saved by grace through faith, not by works (2:8-9). Jews and gentiles are now one household, built on the foundation of the Apostles and prophets, with Jesus Christ Himself as the chief cornerstone (2:19-20). Christ gave Apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers to equip the saints and build up His body (4:11-12). The letter ends with the new life in love, in marriage and in the family, and with the whole armour of God (6:10-18).
themes: Chosen in Christ and sealed with the Holy Spirit (1:4, 13).
Saved by grace, through faith (2:8-9).
One church of Jews and gentiles, built on the Apostles and prophets (2:20).
The ministries Christ gives to build up His body (4:11-12); the Catechism sees them grow out of the Apostle ministry (CNAC 7.5).
Christ and the church, like husband and wife (5:25-27).
parts: What God has done: the church in His plan
How to live: the new life in Christ
EPH.christ: God's plan is to gather together all things in Christ (1:10). Christ is the head of the church, which is His body (1:22-23). He loves her and gave Himself for her, to present her to Himself glorious, without spot or wrinkle (5:25-27).

PHP.title: The letter of Paul to the Philippians
PHP.writer: The Apostle Paul, with Timothy (1:1), writing from prison (1:13).
PHP.when: About AD 60–62, probably from Rome; some think from Ephesus, some years earlier.
PHP.to: The congregation in Philippi, the first in Europe (Acts 16), which loved Paul and had sent him a gift (4:18).
PHP.why: To thank them for their gift, to tell them how he is, to call them to unity and humility, and to warn them against false teachers.
PHP.summary: Although Paul is in chains, joy runs through this letter. “For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (1:21). He calls the congregation to be of one mind and to think as Christ did, who humbled Himself to death on the cross, and whom God highly exalted (2:5-11). Paul counts everything as loss compared with knowing Christ, and presses on toward the goal (3:7-14). Our citizenship is in heaven, from where we wait for the Saviour (3:20-21). “Rejoice in the Lord always” (4:4). “I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me” (4:13).
themes: Joy in every situation (4:4).
The mind of Christ: humility and service (2:5-8).
Pressing on toward the goal (3:14).
