Waiting for the Saviour from heaven (3:20-21).
parts: Paul in prison: to live is Christ
PHP.christ: The hymn in 2:6-11 tells the whole way of Christ: equal with God, He made Himself nothing, became a servant and died on the cross; and God gave Him the name above every name, so that every knee shall bow.

COL.title: The letter of Paul to the Colossians
COL.writer: The Apostle Paul, with Timothy (1:1), writing from prison (4:18). Some scholars think a pupil wrote it.
COL.when: About AD 60–62, at about the same time as Ephesians and Philemon.
COL.to: The congregation in Colossae, a small town in what is now Turkey, founded by Epaphras (1:7). Paul had never been there.
COL.why: To warn against a teaching that added rules, special knowledge and the worship of angels to Christ, and to show that Christ is all we need.
COL.summary: Christ is the image of the invisible God; all things were created through Him and for Him, and in Him all things hold together (1:15-17). In Him dwells all the fullness of God, and in Him we are complete (2:9-10). So do not be led astray by empty philosophy, man-made rules or the worship of angels (2:8, 16-23). Set your mind on things above, where Christ is (3:1-2). Put on the new self: kindness, humility, patience, forgiveness, and above all love (3:12-14). Whatever you do, do it heartily, as to the Lord (3:23).
themes: Christ is above all creation and the head of the church (1:15-18).
In Christ we are complete (2:9-10).
Seek the things above (3:1-2).
The new life in daily life: at home and at work (3:18–4:1).
COL.christ: Colossians gives one of the highest pictures of Christ in the Bible: the firstborn over all creation, the head of the church, the firstborn from the dead (1:15-18). When Christ, who is our life, appears, we will appear with Him in glory (3:4).

1TH.title: The first letter of Paul to the Thessalonians
1TH.writer: The Apostle Paul, with Silvanus and Timothy (1:1).
1TH.when: About AD 50–51, from Corinth. It is probably the oldest of Paul's letters, and so one of the oldest writings of the New Testament (CNAC 1.2.4.1).
1TH.to: The young congregation in Thessalonica, in Greece, which Paul had to leave after only a short time (Acts 17:1-10).
1TH.why: To encourage believers who suffered for their faith, and to comfort them about members who had died before the Lord's return.
1TH.summary: Paul thanks God for the congregation's faith, love and hope: they turned from idols to serve the living God and to wait for His Son from heaven (1:9-10). He reminds them how he lived among them and calls them to a holy life. Then he comforts them: those who have died in Christ are not lost. The Lord Himself will descend from heaven; the dead in Christ will rise first; then we who are alive will be caught up together with them to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord (4:13-18). The day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night, so stay awake (5:1-11).
themes: Faith, love and hope (1:3).
The return of the Lord: the dead in Christ rise first, and the living are caught up to meet Him (4:16-17).
Comfort for those who mourn (4:13, 18).
Stay awake and ready (5:6).
Rejoice, pray, give thanks (5:16-18).
parts: A holy life and the Lord's return
1TH.christ: Every chapter speaks of the Lord's coming (1:10; 2:19; 3:13; 4:17; 5:23). Christ died for us, so that whether we are awake or asleep we shall live together with Him (5:10). This is the hope the Catechism holds out: the return of Christ (CNAC 10.1).

2TH.title: The second letter of Paul to the Thessalonians
2TH.writer: The Apostle Paul, with Silvanus and Timothy (1:1). He signs it with his own hand (3:17). Some scholars think it was written later in his name.
2TH.when: About AD 51, from Corinth, a few months after the first letter.
2TH.why: Some were shaken by the claim that the day of the Lord had already come (2:2), and some had stopped working. Paul calms them, corrects them and calls them to stand firm.
2TH.summary: Paul encourages the congregation in its suffering: when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven, God will set things right (1:6-10). The day of the Lord has not yet come: first the falling away must come, and the man of sin be revealed (2:1-12). So stand firm and hold on to the teaching you were given (2:15). Whoever will not work shall not eat; and do not grow weary in doing good (3:10, 13).
themes: God's justice when the Lord is revealed (1:6-10).
Do not be shaken by false claims about the end (2:2).
Stand firm and hold on to the teaching (2:15).
Work quietly, and do not grow weary in doing good (3:12-13).
parts: The day of the Lord has not yet come
2TH.christ: The Lord Jesus will come to be glorified in His saints (1:10), and will destroy the lawless one with the brightness of His coming (2:8). The Lord is faithful: He will strengthen you and guard you (3:3).

1TI.title: The first letter of Paul to Timothy
1TI.writer: The Apostle Paul (1:1), writing to Timothy, his “true son in the faith” (1:2). Many scholars think the letters to Timothy and Titus were written later, in Paul's name.
1TI.when: About AD 62–64, after Paul's first imprisonment in Rome, if Paul wrote it; later if not.
1TI.to: Timothy, Paul's young co-worker, whom he had left in Ephesus to lead the congregation (1:3).
1TI.why: To guide Timothy in leading the congregation: to stop false teaching, to order the prayers and the divine service, and to say who may serve in the ministry.
1TI.summary: Paul charges Timothy to stand against false teachers and to hold on to faith and a good conscience. He tells of God's mercy to himself, the chief of sinners (1:15). There is one God and one Mediator between God and men, the Man Christ Jesus (2:5). Paul sets out what is asked of those who lead the congregation and of the deacons (chapter 3), and gives advice about widows, elders, slaves and the rich. Timothy must be an example to the believers (4:12), flee the love of money, and fight the good fight of faith (6:10-12).
themes: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners (1:15).
One God and one Mediator (2:5).
What is asked of those who serve in the congregation (chapter 3).
Godliness with contentment; the danger of the love of money (6:6-10).
1TI.christ: “God was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen by angels, preached among the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up in glory” (3:16): an early hymn about Christ.

2TI.title: The second letter of Paul to Timothy
2TI.writer: The Apostle Paul (1:1), in prison in Rome and expecting to die (4:6). Many scholars think it was written later in his name.
2TI.when: About AD 66–67, shortly before Paul's death in Rome, if Paul wrote it.
2TI.why: To encourage Timothy to stay faithful, to guard the gospel, to endure hardship, and to come to him soon.
2TI.summary: This is Paul's last letter. He reminds Timothy of the gift of God that is in him through the laying on of Paul's hands (1:6), for God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, of love and of a sound mind (1:7). Timothy must pass on what he heard to faithful people who will teach others (2:2), endure hardship like a good soldier, and rightly divide the word of truth (2:15). Hard times will come, but all Scripture is given by inspiration of God (3:16). Preach the word; be ready in season and out of season (4:2). Paul looks back: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith” (4:7).
themes: The gift of God through the laying on of hands (1:6).
Pass on the faith to faithful people (2:2).
All Scripture is inspired by God and useful (3:16-17).
Preach the word; finish the race (4:2, 7).
parts: Hard times, Scripture, and Paul's farewell
2TI.christ: Remember that Jesus Christ, of the seed of David, was raised from the dead (2:8). If we died with Him, we shall also live with Him (2:11). Paul waits for the crown of righteousness, which the Lord will give to all who love His appearing (4:8).

TIT.title: The letter of Paul to Titus
TIT.writer: The Apostle Paul (1:1). Many scholars think it was written later in his name.
TIT.when: About AD 63–65, if Paul wrote it.
TIT.to: Titus, a gentile co-worker of Paul (Galatians 2:3), whom he had left on the island of Crete (1:5).
TIT.why: To help Titus set the congregations in order: to appoint elders in every town, to stop false teachers, and to teach a life that fits sound doctrine.
TIT.summary: Paul tells Titus to appoint elders in every city, and says what kind of men they must be (1:5-9). Older and younger men and women, and slaves, are each given guidance for a godly life (chapter 2). For the grace of God has appeared, teaching us to live soberly and godly, while we look for the blessed hope and the glorious appearing of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ (2:11-13). God saved us, not because of our works, but by His mercy, through the washing of regeneration and the renewing of the Holy Spirit (3:5).
themes: Elders appointed in every town (1:5).
A life that fits sound doctrine (2:1).
Grace teaches us while we wait for the blessed hope (2:11-13).
Saved by mercy: rebirth and the Holy Spirit (3:5).
TIT.christ: Titus calls Jesus Christ “our great God and Saviour”, who gave Himself for us to redeem us and to make us His own people (2:13-14). We wait for His glorious appearing.

PHM.title: The letter of Paul to Philemon
PHM.writer: The Apostle Paul, with Timothy (verse 1), writing from prison.
PHM.when: About AD 60–62, at the same time as Colossians.
PHM.to: Philemon, a believer in Colossae, in whose house the congregation met (verse 2).
PHM.why: To ask Philemon to take back his runaway slave Onesimus, who had come to faith through Paul, no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother.
PHM.summary: Onesimus had run away from his master Philemon, perhaps after stealing from him. He met Paul in prison and came to faith. Paul sends him back with this short letter. He does not order Philemon, but asks him in love to receive Onesimus as he would receive Paul himself. If Onesimus owes him anything, Paul will pay it (verses 18-19).
themes: In Christ a slave becomes a brother (verse 16).
Forgiveness and a new start.
Asking in love rather than giving orders (verses 8-9).
PHM.christ: Paul's offer, “put that on my account” (verse 18), is a picture of what Christ did for us: He took our debt upon Himself, and brings us back to the Father as His own.

HEB.title: The letter to the Hebrews
HEB.writer: Not named. Some in the early church thought of Paul; others of Barnabas, Apollos or Luke. The church father Origen said: only God knows who wrote it.
HEB.when: Probably before AD 70, since it speaks of the sacrifices of the old covenant as still going on (10:1-2).
HEB.to: Jewish Christians who were tempted to give up and go back to their old ways (10:35-39).
HEB.why: To show that Jesus is greater than the angels, than Moses and than the priests of the old covenant, and to call the readers to hold on to their faith.
HEB.summary: God, who spoke in many ways through the prophets, has in these last days spoken to us by His Son (1:1-2). Jesus is greater than the angels and than Moses. He is the great High Priest who understands our weakness, because He was tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin (4:15). He is a priest for ever in the order of Melchizedek (chapter 7). With His own blood He entered the holy place once for all, and obtained eternal redemption (9:12). Chapter 11 is the roll call of faith: Abel, Noah, Abraham, Moses and many more. So let us run the race with endurance, looking to Jesus (12:1-2).
themes: Jesus is greater than the angels, Moses and the priests of old (chapters 1–7).
The one sacrifice of Christ, once for all (9:12; 10:10).
The new covenant (8:8-12).
Faith: being sure of what we hope for (11:1).
Hold on, do not give up (10:23; 12:1-2).
parts: The Son is greater than the angels and Moses
Jesus the High Priest and His one sacrifice
HEB.christ: Hebrews shows Christ as the fulfilment of all the worship of the Old Testament: the true High Priest and the true sacrifice. He will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to save those who eagerly wait for Him (9:28).

JAS.title: The letter of James
JAS.writer: James (1:1), usually held to be the brother of the Lord (Galatians 1:19), who led the congregation in Jerusalem (Acts 15:13).
JAS.when: Probably before AD 62, the year James was killed; some date it as early as AD 45–50.
JAS.to: “The twelve tribes which are scattered abroad” (1:1): Jewish Christians living outside the land of Israel.
JAS.why: To show that true faith is seen in how we live: in patience, in what we say, in caring for the poor, and in prayer.
JAS.summary: James is full of practical wisdom, much like Proverbs and the Sermon on the Mount. Count it joy when your faith is tested (1:2-3). If you lack wisdom, ask God (1:5). Be doers of the word, and not hearers only (1:22). Do not favour the rich above the poor (2:1-9). Faith without works is dead (2:17, 26). The tongue is small, but it can set a whole forest on fire (3:5-6). Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you (4:8). Is anyone sick? Let him call for the elders of the church to pray over him (5:14). The prayer of a righteous person has great power (5:16).
themes: Trials that make faith grow (1:2-4).
Hearing and doing the word (1:22).
Faith and works belong together (2:17). Paul and James do not contradict each other: true faith shows itself in what it does.
Taming the tongue (chapter 3).
Prayer for the sick and for one another (5:13-16).
parts: Trials, wisdom and doing the word
JAS.christ: James names Jesus only twice (1:1; 2:1), but his letter echoes Jesus' own teaching again and again. He calls believers to be patient until the coming of the Lord, for it is near (5:7-8).

1PE.title: The first letter of Peter
1PE.writer: The Apostle Peter (1:1), with the help of Silvanus (5:12). Some scholars think it was written later, in his name.
1PE.when: About AD 62–64, from “Babylon” (5:13), probably meaning Rome, before Peter's death under Emperor Nero.
1PE.to: Believers scattered across what is now Turkey (1:1), who suffered for their faith.
1PE.why: To give hope and courage to Christians who suffered, and to show them how to live as God's people in a hostile world.
1PE.summary: God has given us new birth to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ (1:3). Our faith is tested like gold in the fire (1:7). We are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God's own people (2:9). Live well among unbelievers, and follow Christ's example in suffering (2:21). Christ suffered once for sins, the just for the unjust, and went and preached to the spirits in prison (3:18-19); the gospel was preached also to the dead (4:6). Elders must shepherd the flock willingly (5:2). Cast all your care on God, for He cares for you (5:7).
themes: A living hope through Christ's resurrection (1:3).
God's own people: a royal priesthood (2:9).
Suffering for doing good, following Christ's example (2:21).
The gospel preached also to the dead (3:18-20; 4:6). The Catechism sees here the help for the departed (CNAC 9.6.3).
Shepherding the flock of God (5:1-4).
parts: A living hope; God's own people
Living among unbelievers; suffering like Christ
Suffering, the elders and the flock
1PE.christ: Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example (2:21); He bore our sins in His own body on the tree (2:24). He is the Shepherd and Overseer of our souls (2:25), and His work reaches even into the realm of the dead (3:19; 4:6).

2PE.title: The second letter of Peter
2PE.writer: The Apostle Peter (1:1), an eyewitness of Jesus' transfiguration (1:16-18), who knew his death was near (1:14). Many scholars think it was written later, in his name.
2PE.when: About AD 64–68, shortly before Peter's death, if Peter wrote it.
2PE.to: Believers who share the same precious faith (1:1), probably the same readers as the first letter (3:1).
2PE.why: To call believers to grow in faith, to warn against false teachers, and to answer those who mocked: “Where is the promise of His coming?” (3:4).
2PE.summary: God's power has given us all things that we need for life and godliness (1:3). So add to your faith virtue, knowledge, self-control, patience, godliness, brotherly kindness and love (1:5-7). Peter reminds them that he saw Christ's glory with his own eyes, and that no prophecy of Scripture came by the will of man: holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit (1:21). False teachers will come (chapter 2). Some mock the promise of the Lord's coming, but with the Lord one day is as a thousand years. He is not slow; He is patient, not wanting anyone to be lost (3:8-9). We look for new heavens and a new earth (3:13).
themes: Grow in faith, step by step (1:5-8).
Scripture given through the Holy Spirit (1:20-21).
A warning against false teachers (chapter 2).
The Lord's coming is sure; His delay is patience (3:9).
parts: Grow in faith; the sure word
The day of the Lord will come
2PE.christ: Peter saw Christ's majesty on the holy mountain and heard the Father's voice: “This is My beloved Son” (1:17). The letter ends: grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ (3:18).

1JN.title: The first letter of John
1JN.writer: Not named in the letter. The early church held it to be the Apostle John, who wrote the gospel; the words are very close to John's gospel.
1JN.to: Congregations John knew well; he calls them “my little children” (2:1).
1JN.why: Some had left the congregation and taught that Jesus had not truly come in the flesh. John writes so that believers may know that they have eternal life (5:13), and keep walking in the light and in love.
1JN.summary: John begins with what he heard, saw and touched: the Word of life (1:1). God is light; if we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us (1:9). Whoever says he knows God must keep His commandments and love his brother. See what love the Father has given us, that we should be called children of God; when He appears, we shall be like Him (3:1-2). Test the spirits: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is of God (4:2). God is love, and we love Him because He first loved us (4:8, 19).
themes: Walking in the light; confessing our sins (1:7-9).
God is love; love one another (4:7-8).
Jesus Christ has truly come in the flesh (4:2).
When He appears, we shall be like Him (3:2).
Certainty: you may know that you have eternal life (5:13).
1JN.christ: Jesus Christ the righteous is our Advocate with the Father and the atoning sacrifice for our sins (2:1-2). God sent His only Son into the world, so that we might live through Him (4:9).

2JN.title: The second letter of John
2JN.writer: “The elder” (verse 1), held by the early church to be the Apostle John.
2JN.when: About AD 85–95, at about the same time as 1 John.
2JN.to: “The elect lady and her children” (verse 1): probably a congregation and its members.
2JN.why: To call the congregation to walk in truth and love, and to warn it not to welcome teachers who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh.
2JN.summary: In this short letter John rejoices that some of the congregation walk in the truth. He repeats the old commandment: love one another (verse 5). And this is love: that we walk according to God's commandments (verse 6). Many deceivers have gone out who do not confess that Jesus Christ came in the flesh; do not receive them into your house (verses 7-10).
themes: Truth and love belong together (verse 3).
Love one another (verse 5).
Stay in the teaching of Christ (verse 9).
2JN.christ: Whoever stays in the teaching of Christ has both the Father and the Son (verse 9). Confessing that Jesus Christ came in the flesh is the mark of the truth (verse 7).

3JN.title: The third letter of John
3JN.writer: “The elder” (verse 1), held to be the Apostle John.
3JN.to: Gaius, a dear friend in one of the congregations (verse 1).
3JN.why: To thank Gaius for receiving brothers who travelled for the gospel, to warn about Diotrephes, who wanted to be first and turned them away, and to commend Demetrius.
3JN.summary: John wishes Gaius good health, just as his soul is well (verse 2). He has no greater joy than to hear that his children walk in the truth (verse 4). Gaius is faithful in caring for the brothers who travel for the sake of the Name. Diotrephes, who loves to be first, does not receive them, and even puts others out of the congregation. “Do not imitate what is evil, but what is good” (verse 11).
themes: Joy over those who walk in the truth (verse 4).
Hospitality to God's servants (verses 5-8).
Pride in the congregation does harm (verses 9-10).
3JN.christ: The brothers went out “for His name's sake” (verse 7): the name of Christ is the reason for their journeys and for the welcome they are given.

JUD.title: The letter of Jude
JUD.writer: Jude, “a servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James” (verse 1), usually held to be a brother of the Lord (Mark 6:3).
JUD.when: About AD 65–80. It is close to chapter 2 of 2 Peter.
JUD.to: Those who are called, loved by God and kept for Jesus Christ (verse 1).
JUD.why: Jude had wanted to write about our shared salvation, but had to warn instead: ungodly people had crept in, who used God's grace as an excuse to sin (verses 3-4).
JUD.summary: Contend earnestly for the faith which was once for all delivered to the saints (verse 3). Jude reminds his readers of God's judgement in the past: on Israel in the desert, on the angels who fell, and on Sodom and Gomorrah. The false teachers are like clouds without water and trees without fruit (verse 12). But you, beloved, build yourselves up in your most holy faith, pray in the Holy Spirit, and keep yourselves in the love of God, waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ (verses 20-21). The letter ends with a well-known blessing: to Him who is able to keep you from stumbling (verses 24-25).
themes: Contend for the faith (verse 3).
God judges those who turn grace into sin (verse 4).
Keep yourselves in God's love (verse 21).
God is able to keep you (verse 24).
JUD.christ: Believers are kept for Jesus Christ (verse 1) and wait for His mercy unto eternal life (verse 21). Jude quotes the old prophecy: “Behold, the Lord comes with ten thousands of His saints” (verse 14).

REV.title: The Revelation of Jesus Christ to John
REV.writer: John (1:1, 4, 9), on the island of Patmos, where he was banished because of the word of God. The early church held him to be the Apostle John.
REV.when: About AD 95, near the end of Emperor Domitian's rule, when Christians were persecuted; some date it about AD 68.
REV.to: Seven congregations in the province of Asia, now Turkey (1:4), and through them the whole church.
REV.why: To comfort and strengthen a suffering church: Christ has won, God holds history in His hand, and the Lord is coming soon.
REV.summary: John sees the risen Christ among seven lampstands and writes letters to seven congregations (chapters 1–3). Then he sees God's throne in heaven and the Lamb who was slain, who alone may open the scroll with seven seals (chapters 4–5). Seals, trumpets and bowls show God's judgements on a world that resists Him, and the fight of the dragon and the beasts against God's people (chapters 6–18). Then heaven rejoices: the marriage of the Lamb has come (19:7). Christ appears; those who have part in the first resurrection reign with Him a thousand years (20:6). After the last judgement God makes all things new: a new heaven and a new earth, where He will wipe away every tear (21:4). “Surely I am coming quickly.” “Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus!” (22:20).
themes: Christ has won: the Lamb who was slain is worthy (5:12).
The letters to the seven congregations: words for the church in every age (chapters 2–3).
The marriage of the Lamb and the first resurrection (19:7-9; 20:6).
God makes all things new (21:5).
The Lord is coming soon (22:20).
parts: Seals, trumpets and bowls: judgement on a resisting world
Christ's victory, the first resurrection and the last judgement
A new heaven and a new earth
REV.christ: Revelation shows Christ as the First and the Last (1:17), the Lamb who was slain and is worthy (5:12), the Bridegroom (19:7) and the King of kings (19:16). Here the Catechism finds the hope of the Church: Christ's return for His bride, the marriage of the Lamb and the first resurrection (CNAC 10.1, 10.2 and 10.5).
